intro: You have two cookies. A friend gives you three more. How many now? Your sister takes one. How many are left? These are adding and subtracting questions. You meet them every day, at lunch, at recess and at the store.

In this unit you will put groups together and take groups apart. You will learn what the equal sign really means. You will find a missing number in any spot. Then you will learn quick tricks: doubles, making ten and fact families.
By the end, you will know your facts within 20. You will solve story problems with two steps. And you will check your answer a second way, so you know it is right.
bigQuestion: How do we put numbers together, take them apart, and know the answer is right?

timeline.t: Put two groups together and count them all
Count on from the first number instead of starting at 1
Take some away and count what is left
Compare two groups to find how many more
Split a whole into two parts with a number bond
Read the equal sign as the same as, and find a missing number
Learn doubles and the pairs that make ten
Use near doubles and make ten to add within 20
Think addition to subtract, and build fact families
Solve two-step stories and check the answer a second way

to take some away and find how many are left
the answer when you add; 3 + 2 = 5, so 5 is the sum
the answer when you subtract; 7 − 3 = 4, so 4 is the difference
a picture with a whole and its two parts; 10 has parts 7 and 3
the same amount; the = sign says both sides match
break one number so a part of it fills the other up to 10
four facts that use the same three numbers, two adding and two subtracting

test.why: Draw 9 circles. Cross out 5. Four are left. 9 − 5 = 4.

test.q: The whole is 10. One part is 3. What is the other part?

test.why: 2 + 3 = 5, so both sides are 5. The others make 4 and 6.
Count on from 4 to 9: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. Five jumps. 4 + 5 = 9.
Think 5 + ? = 12. From 5, jump 5 to 10, then 2 to 12. 5 + 2 = 7.

test.q: Which fact is in the family with 6 + 9 = 15?
test.why: The whole is 15. 15 − 6 = 9 uses the same three numbers.

test.q: Bo has 9 rocks. He finds 5 more. Then he gives 6 away. How many now?

write.prompt: Mia has 7 stickers. She gets 6 more. Then she gives 4 to a friend. How many stickers does Mia have now? Solve it one step at a time. Then check your answer a second way.
tips: Write a number sentence for step 1.
Write a number sentence for step 2.
Tell which trick you used, like make ten or count on.
Check it a second way and say if it matches.

title: Adding and Subtracting

chapters.title: Putting Together and Taking Apart
chapters.bigQuestion: How do numbers change when we put groups together or take some away?

story.title: Nine Ducks on the Pond
story.kicker: Count the ducks before and after some fly away.
paragraphs: Nine ducks float on a pond in a Chicago park. A girl named Rosa counts them from the path. One, two, three, all the way to nine. She writes 9 on her hand with her finger so she will not forget.
A dog barks. Four ducks flap their wings and fly away. Rosa looks again. Some ducks are gone. How many stay on the water? She counts them: five ducks. Nine take away four is five.
Later, two ducks come back. Rosa counts again. Five and two more. Now there are seven ducks. The number went down, then it went up. Taking away and putting together, right there on the pond.
story.think: How could Rosa know there are 5 ducks without counting every duck again?

lessons.title: Adding Puts Groups Together
lessons.mainIdea: Adding puts two groups together to find how many in all.
reading: Mia has 3 red apples. Ben has 2 green apples. Put them in one basket. Count them all: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. There are 5 apples in all. We *add* the two groups.
We write it like this: 3 + 2 = 5. The + sign means put together. The answer is called the *sum*. Five is the sum of 3 and 2.
Try 4 + 3. Start with 4 blocks. Add 3 more blocks. Count them all. You get 7. So 4 + 3 = 7.

words.d: to put groups together and find how many in all
the answer when you add; 3 + 2 = 5, so 5 is the sum

look.title: Two Piles of Blocks
look.text: Look at two piles of blocks on a table. The first pile has 5 blocks. The second pile has 3 blocks. Push the piles together. Now count every block. Start at 1 and say each number out loud.
look.prompt: How many blocks are there in all? Write the adding sentence.

check.q: Ana has 2 cats. Leo has 4 cats. How many cats in all?

check.why: The + sign means add, or put together. The − sign means take away.
3 blocks and 3 more blocks make 6 blocks. 3 + 3 = 6.

lessons.title: Adding More to a Group
lessons.mainIdea: When more come, say the first number and count on.
reading: Six birds sit on a fence. Two more birds land. How many birds now? Start at 6. Count on: 7, 8. There are 8 birds. 6 + 2 = 8.
You do not need to count from 1. Say the first number. Then count on for the other part. This is called *counting on*. It is faster.
Try 5 + 3. Say 5. Count on three times: 6, 7, 8. The sum is 8. Check it with fingers. Five fingers and three more make 8.

words.d: start at one number and count up from there; for 6 + 2, say 6, then 7, 8

look.title: The Bus Stop
look.text: Four kids wait at a bus stop. Three more kids walk up. Picture the four kids first. Then picture the three new kids joining them. Say 4, then count on one number for each new kid.
look.prompt: How many kids are at the bus stop now? Say the counting on numbers.

check.q: 7 fish are in a tank. 2 more go in. How many fish now?
To find 8 + 3 by counting on, what number do you say first?
check.why: Start at 8. Then count on three times: 9, 10, 11.
Say 5, then count on four times: 6, 7, 8, 9. So 5 + 4 = 9.

lessons.title: Taking Away
lessons.mainIdea: Subtracting takes some away and finds how many are left.
reading: Sam has 7 grapes. He eats 3. How many are left? Start with 7. Take away 3. Count what is left: 4. We *subtract*. 7 − 3 = 4.
The − sign means take away. The answer is called the *difference*. Four is the difference between 7 and 3.
Try 9 − 4. Draw 9 circles. Cross out 4. Count the circles not crossed out. There are 5. So 9 − 4 = 5.

words.d: to take some away and find how many are left
the answer when you subtract; 7 − 3 = 4, so 4 is the difference

look.title: Cookies on a Plate
look.text: Picture a plate with 8 cookies. Two friends each take one cookie. Now look at the plate again. Two cookies left the plate. Count the cookies that are still there.
look.prompt: How many cookies are left? Write the subtracting sentence.

check.q: There are 6 balloons. 2 pop. How many are left?

check.why: The − sign means subtract, or take away.
Draw 10 circles. Cross out 6. Four are left. 10 − 6 = 4.

lessons.title: How Many More?
lessons.mainIdea: Subtract to compare two groups and find how many more.
reading: Jo has 8 stickers. Kim has 5. Who has more? Jo. How many more? Line them up. Match each of Kim's stickers to one of Jo's. Three of Jo's stickers have no match. Jo has 3 more.
We can subtract to *compare*. 8 − 5 = 3. The bigger number goes first. Then take away the smaller number. The difference tells how many *more*.
Try it. A tower has 6 blocks. Another has 2. How many more in the tall tower? 6 − 2 = 4. The tall tower has 4 more blocks.

words.d: to look at two groups and find which is bigger and by how much
a bigger amount; 8 is more than 5

look.title: Pets at Home
look.cite: Example table made for this lesson
look.prompt: How many more dogs than fish are there? Subtract to find out.

check.q: Ria has 9 shells. Tom has 4. How many more does Ria have?
check.why: 9 − 4 = 5. Match 4 of Ria's shells to Tom's. Five are left over.

check.q: The pet table shows 6 dogs and 4 cats. How many more dogs than cats?
check.why: 6 − 4 = 2. There are 2 more dogs than cats.
To compare, put the bigger number first and subtract. 7 − 3 = 4.

lessons.title: Parts and the Whole
lessons.mainIdea: A number bond shows a whole and its two parts.
reading: Hold up 7 fingers. Keep 3 down. The parts are 7 and 3. The *whole* is 10. A *number bond* shows this. The whole sits on top. The two parts sit below. 10 splits into 7 and 3.
The parts always add up to the whole. 7 + 3 = 10. The whole minus one *part* gives the other part. 10 − 7 = 3.
Find the parts of 5. 1 and 4. 2 and 3. 0 and 5. Each pair makes 5. Try it with 5 counters. Split them two ways.

words.d: a picture with a whole and its two parts; 10 has parts 7 and 3
the total; the big number in a number bond
one piece of the whole; 7 and 3 are parts of 10

look.title: Break the Tower
look.text: Picture a tower of 6 blocks. Break it into two smaller towers. Maybe 4 and 2. Maybe 5 and 1. Maybe 3 and 3. Each time, the two small towers still make 6 in all.
look.prompt: Name all the ways to break 6 into two parts. How many ways do you find?

check.q: The whole is 8. One part is 5. What is the other part?
A number bond has whole 9 and part 6. What is the missing part?

lessons.title: What Equals Means
lessons.mainIdea: The equal sign means both sides are the same amount.
reading: Two plates. One has 3 crackers and 2 more. The other has 5 crackers. Both plates hold 5. They are *equal*. 3 + 2 = 5. The = sign means the same as.
The equal sign is not just an answer sign. It says both sides match. 5 = 3 + 2 is *true*. 4 + 1 = 3 + 2 is true too. Both sides make 5.
Is 6 = 2 + 3 true? Count 2 + 3. That is 5. Six is not 5. So it is false. Check both sides every time.

words.d: the same amount; 3 + 2 = 5 means 3 + 2 is the same as 5
correct; both sides of the equal sign really match

look.title: The Balance Scale
look.text: Picture a balance scale, like a seesaw. Put 4 blocks and 2 blocks on the left side. Put 6 blocks on the right side. The scale sits level. Both sides weigh the same. Now take one block off the right side.
look.prompt: Is 4 + 2 = 6 true? What happens to the scale after you take a block off?

check.why: The equal sign says both sides are the same amount.
2 + 4 = 6 and 3 + 3 = 6. Both sides are 6, so it is true.

lessons.title: Find the Missing Number
lessons.mainIdea: A missing number can be in any spot; use parts and wholes to find it.
reading: Dan has 3 marbles. He gets some more. Now he has 7. How many did he get? 3 + ? = 7. Count on from 3 to 7: 4, 5, 6, 7. That is 4 jumps. So 3 + 4 = 7.
The *missing number* can be in any spot. ? + 2 = 6. Think: what and 2 make 6? Four. Or 8 − ? = 5. Think: 8 take away what leaves 5? Three, since 5 + 3 = 8.
Use a number bond. The whole is 7. One part is 3. The other part is 7 − 3 = 4. Subtracting finds the missing part.

words.d: the number you do not know yet, shown by a ? or a box
another name for the missing number

look.title: The Mystery Box
look.text: Picture a box with 5 marbles inside. A friend drops in a handful. Now you count 9 marbles. You did not see how many went in. But you know the start and the end. Count up from 5 to 9.
look.prompt: How many marbles did your friend drop in? Write the sentence with a ? for the missing number.

check.why: Count on from 5 to 9: 6, 7, 8, 9. Four jumps. 5 + 4 = 9.

lessons.title: Doubles and Making Ten
lessons.mainIdea: Doubles and pairs that make ten are facts worth knowing by heart.
reading: Two hands. Five fingers each. 5 + 5 = 10. That is a *double*. Both parts are the same. 2 + 2 = 4. 3 + 3 = 6. 4 + 4 = 8. Doubles are quick to learn.
Pairs that *make ten* are handy too. Hold up 6 fingers. How many are down? Four. So 6 + 4 = 10. Other pairs: 9 and 1, 8 and 2, 7 and 3, 5 and 5.
What goes with 8 to make 10? Hold up 8 fingers. Two are down. 8 + 2 = 10. Check by counting on from 8: 9, 10. Yes.

words.d: adding a number to itself, like 4 + 4 = 8
two numbers that add up to 10, like 7 and 3

look.title: Doubles Chart
look.prompt: What pattern do you see in the sums? What would 6 + 6 be?

check.why: 4 + 4 = 8. It is a double: 4 fingers and 4 fingers.
A double adds a number to itself. 6 + 6 = 12.

review.q: There are 4 ducks. 3 more swim over. How many ducks now?
There are 9 ducks. 4 fly away. How many are left?
Which sign means the same as?
review.why: The = sign means both sides are the same amount.

review.q: The whole is 10. One part is 6. What is the other part?

review.why: Count on from 2 to 8: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Six jumps. 2 + 6 = 8.

review.q: Lucy has 7 shells. Max has 3. How many more does Lucy have?
review.why: 7 − 3 = 4. Lucy has 4 more shells than Max.

chapters.title: Facts Within 20 and Good Strategies
chapters.bigQuestion: What tricks help you know adding and subtracting facts fast?

story.title: The Fact House on the Wall
story.kicker: A paper house holds four facts that all belong together.
paragraphs: Mr. Ortiz's first-grade class has a paper house on the wall. The roof says 10. The two windows say 6 and 4. The door has four lines on it. Each line is a number fact. The class reads the house every morning.
Deshawn reads the door out loud. 6 + 4 = 10. 4 + 6 = 10. 10 − 6 = 4. 10 − 4 = 6. Every line uses the same three numbers. That is why the facts live in one house. They are a family.
On Friday the roof number changes to 13. The windows say 8 and 5. Deshawn writes the four new facts by himself. He knows one fact, so he knows all four. The house makes facts easy to remember.
story.think: Why do the three numbers in the house make exactly four facts?

lessons.title: Count On to Add
lessons.mainIdea: To add a small number, start with the big number and count on.
reading: Nine kids wait in line for the slide. Three more join. Say 9. *Count on*: 10, 11, 12. There are 12 kids. 9 + 3 = 12.
Always start with the bigger number. For 2 + 8, say 8 first. Count on: 9, 10. The sum is 10. The *order* does not change the sum. 2 + 8 = 8 + 2.
Use counting on for 1, 2 or 3. For bigger numbers, use another trick. Try 11 + 2. Say 11. Then 12, 13. So 11 + 2 = 13.

words.d: start at the bigger number and count up from there
which number comes first; 2 + 8 and 8 + 2 have the same sum

look.title: Hops on the Number Line
look.text: Picture a number line from 0 to 20. Put your finger on 14. Now hop 3 times to the right. Say each number you land on. The last number you land on is the sum.
look.prompt: Where do you land? Write the adding sentence for 14 + 3.

check.q: To add 3 + 9 by counting on, which number do you say first?
check.why: Start with the bigger number, 9. Then count on: 10, 11, 12.

lessons.title: Count Back to Subtract
lessons.mainIdea: To take away a small number, start at the whole and count back.
reading: Eleven cookies sit on a tray. Grandpa eats 2. Say 11. *Count back*: 10, 9. Nine cookies are left. 11 − 2 = 9.
Count back only for 1, 2 or 3. Use your fingers to keep track. Each finger is one step back. For 13 − 3, say 13. Back: 12, 11, 10. The difference is 10.
A common mistake is to say the start number as a step. 11 − 2 is not 10. Start at 11. Step to 10, then to 9. Two steps. The answer is 9.

words.d: start at the whole and count down one step for each one taken away

look.title: Steps Down the Stairs
look.text: You stand on stair 16. You step down 3 stairs. Say the number of each stair you step onto: 15, then 14, then 13. Think of each step as taking one away.
look.prompt: Which stair do you end on? Write it as a subtracting sentence.

check.q: Nina has 17 beads. She gives away 2. How many are left?

check.why: One step back from 12 is 11. So 12 − 1 = 11.

lessons.title: Near Doubles
lessons.mainIdea: If you know a double, you can find the fact right next to it.
reading: You know 6 + 6 = 12. What is 6 + 7? Seven is one more than 6. So the sum is one more than 12. 6 + 7 = 13. That is a *near double*.
Try 8 + 9. Think 8 + 8 = 16. Nine is one more than 8. So 8 + 9 = 17. Or think 9 + 9 = 18 and take one away. That gives 17 again.
Doubles to know: 6 + 6 = 12, 7 + 7 = 14, 8 + 8 = 16, 9 + 9 = 18, 10 + 10 = 20. Near doubles are one more or one less.

words.d: a fact one more or one less than a double, like 6 + 7

look.title: Doubles and Near Doubles
look.prompt: Each near double is how much more than its double? Use that to find 8 + 9.

lessons.title: Make Ten to Add
lessons.mainIdea: Break one number so the other becomes 10, then add the rest.
reading: Add 8 + 5. Eight is close to 10. It needs 2 more. Take 2 from the 5. Now 8 + 2 = 10. Three are left from the 5. 10 + 3 = 13. So 8 + 5 = 13. This is called *make ten*.
Picture a *ten frame*. Eight dots fill 8 spots. Two spots are empty. Move 2 dots from the 5 to fill them. The frame is full: 10. Three dots wait outside. Ten and 3 is 13.
Try 9 + 6. Nine needs 1. Take 1 from 6. 9 + 1 = 10. Five are left. 10 + 5 = 15. So 9 + 6 = 15. Check by counting on from 9: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15. Yes.

words.d: break one number so a part of it fills the other number up to 10
a box with 10 spots in two rows of 5

look.title: Fill the Frame
look.text: Picture a ten frame with 7 dots. Three spots are empty. Next to it sit 4 loose dots. Slide 3 of the loose dots into the empty spots. The frame is full. Count the loose dots still outside.
look.prompt: How many dots are there in all? What is 7 + 4?

check.q: Add 8 + 4 by making ten. How many do you move from the 4?
check.why: 8 needs 2 to make 10. Move 2 from the 4. Then 10 + 2 = 12.

lessons.title: Think Addition to Subtract
lessons.mainIdea: To subtract, ask what you add to the part to reach the whole.
reading: What is 13 − 9? Think: 9 plus what makes 13? *Count up* from 9: 10, 11, 12, 13. Four jumps. 9 + 4 = 13. So 13 − 9 = 4.
This works because adding and subtracting *undo* each other. If 9 + 4 = 13, then 13 − 9 = 4 and 13 − 4 = 9. All three facts share the same parts.
Try 15 − 8. Think 8 + ? = 15. From 8, jump 2 to reach 10. Then jump 5 to reach 15. 2 + 5 = 7. So 15 − 8 = 7. Check: 8 + 7 = 15. Yes.

words.d: start at the part and count to the whole to find the difference
adding undoes subtracting; 9 + 4 = 13, so 13 − 4 = 9

look.title: The Missing Pieces
look.text: A puzzle has 12 pieces. You have snapped 8 into place. Picture the empty gap. Count up from 8 until you reach 12: 9, 10, 11, 12. Each number you say is one missing piece.
look.prompt: How many pieces are missing? Write the subtracting sentence and the adding sentence.

check.why: Count up from 9: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14. Five jumps. 9 + 5 = 14, so 14 − 9 = 5.

check.q: To find 11 − 7, which adding question helps?
check.why: Ask 7 plus what makes 11? That is 4. So 11 − 7 = 4.

lessons.title: Fact Families
lessons.mainIdea: Three numbers make a family of two adding facts and two subtracting facts.
reading: Take 4, 6 and 10. Ten is the whole. Four and 6 are the parts. Write four facts: 4 + 6 = 10. 6 + 4 = 10. 10 − 4 = 6. 10 − 6 = 4. This is a *fact family*.
The whole is always the sum. The whole comes first in the subtracting facts. If you know one fact, you know all four.
Try 5, 8 and 13. Adding: 5 + 8 = 13 and 8 + 5 = 13. Subtracting: 13 − 5 = 8 and 13 − 8 = 5. A double like 7 + 7 = 14 has only two facts. Both parts match.

words.d: four facts that use the same three numbers, two adding and two subtracting

look.title: The Fact House
look.text: Picture a house shape. The number 12 sits in the roof. The numbers 5 and 7 sit in the two windows. Four lines are written on the door. Each line uses all three numbers, and the roof number is the whole.
look.prompt: Write the four facts on the door for 5, 7 and 12.

check.q: Which fact is in the family of 3, 9 and 12?
check.why: 12 is the whole. 12 − 3 = 9 is true. The whole comes first when subtracting.

check.q: A family has 2 + 7 = 9. Which subtracting fact belongs?
check.why: The whole is 9. 9 − 7 = 2 uses the same three numbers.

check.q: How many facts are in the family of 6, 8 and 14?

lessons.title: Two-Step Story Problems
lessons.mainIdea: Solve one step at a time, then check by a second way.
reading: Ava has 8 crayons. She gets 5 more. Then she gives 3 to Ben. How many now? Step 1: 8 + 5 = 13. Step 2: 13 − 3 = 10. Ava has 10 crayons. This is a *two-step problem*.
Read the story twice. Find the first thing that happens. Do that step. Then use its answer for the next step. Write both number sentences.
*Check* by a second way. Ava got 5 and gave away 3. That is 2 more overall. 8 + 2 = 10. Same answer. Two ways, same answer, so it is right.

words.d: a story problem with two things to do, one after the other
solve again a different way to see if the answers match

look.title: The Lemonade Stand
look.text: You have 12 cups. You sell 4 cups of lemonade. Then a friend brings 6 more cups. Picture the pile of cups after each thing that happens. Write a number sentence for each step.
look.prompt: How many cups do you have at the end? Check it a second way.

check.q: Joe has 6 cars. He gets 4 more. Then he loses 2. How many now?
15 birds sit in a tree. 6 fly away. Then 3 come back. What is the first step?
check.why: First 6 fly away, so subtract: 15 − 6 = 9. Then add the 3 that come back.

check.q: 15 birds. 6 fly away. Then 3 come back. How many birds now?

review.why: Think 8 + ? = 17. From 8, jump 2 to 10, then 7 to 17. 2 + 7 = 9.
8 + 8 is a double. Both parts are the same. 8 + 8 = 16.

review.q: Which fact belongs to the family of 4, 7 and 11?
9 + 6: take 1 from the 6 to make ten. What is left to add?
Ken has 10 stickers. He gives 4 away. Then he gets 7. How many now?
